conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the EPDS, a short 10-item questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s not a test of your parenting; it simply gives us a snapshot of your emotional wellbeing so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and we’ll take it at your pace.

I’ll ask each question conversationally, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. When you’re ready, here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly, I’ve still been able to laugh. My husband or my mom will say something silly and I’ll catch myself giggling—especially when the baby makes those funny milk-drunk faces. It might not be as often as before, because I’m tired, but the laughter is still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my little guy flashes that gummy smile or my partner does something goofy, I definitely chuckle.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most days I do find myself looking forward to little things—like taking the baby for a walk in the stroller or having my morning coffee once my husband gets up. They’re small, but they still feel nice.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a ton or won’t settle, I figure it’s just part of the newborn phase, not something I’m doing wrong. I might shrug and say, “Well, babies are unpredictable,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I do feel a wave of worry out of nowhere—like I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay while he’s napping, even though I can see the monitor and everything looks fine. It passes pretty quickly, though.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I haven’t had any real panic moments—maybe a quick flutter of “what if?” when I hear him make a weird grunt in his sleep, but it’s gone in a second, and I haven’t felt truly scared or panicky.
Things have been getting on top of me

A couple of times I’ve felt like the to-do list is stacking up faster than I can cross things off—laundry, bottles, texts to return—but I take a breath, handle one thing at a time, and it feels manageable again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been fine—once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly. I’m tired, but it’s more from the night feeds than from feeling unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t say I feel sad or miserable—just a little worn out. Most of the day I’m okay, maybe a bit teary when I’m really tired, but it lifts once I rest or someone helps with the baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve only teared up once or twice, and it was more from exhaustion than feeling truly unhappy. It passed quickly—no real crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. That hasn’t crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS Responses Review

Symptoms endorsed
- Occasional “wave of worry” without clear trigger; resolves quickly  
- Transient sense of tasks “stacking up” but regains control with self-soothing

Symptoms denied
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, self-blame, panic episodes, sleep-onset problems linked to mood, crying spells, suicidal or self-harm ideation

Pattern
Overall mood remains positive with intact capacity for enjoyment and laughter; anxiety symptoms are mild, situation-specific, and self-limited. No evidence of significant depressive or safety concern at this time.

Screening significance
Findings do not meet threshold indicators for major postpartum depression; mild situational anxiety may warrant psycho-education and routine re-screening at next visit.
